#4638. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4637. Inside Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center, which doles out 10,000 pounds of food every day

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Cases of peanut butter, bright red boxes of Shredded Wheat cereal, and so many varieties of tea that even Mary Poppins would be excited. Around the corner, large wooden crates teeming with wide leaves and sturdy grasses, and a walk-in refrigerator full of fresh produce sit ready to turn into dishes that are a feast for the eyes and the belly.

For the team working at Disney’s Animal Nutrition Center (ANC) at Walt Disney World Resort in Orlando, Florida, it’s like Thanksgiving every day. The roughly 40 cast members on the animal nutrition team is responsible for feeding the over 5,000 animals at Disney’s Animal Kingdom Theme Park and The Seas at EPCOT. It takes time, a devotion to the science of nutrition, and really knowing your audience to deliver about 10,000 pounds of food per day. And like putting together any big meal, it requires a team effort, which extends well beyond the animals at Disney.

“What we’re trying to do is provide the optimal nutrition for animals to live long and healthy lives, and we do that by taking information from a lot of different fields,” Animal Nutrition Operations Manager Dr. Heidi Bissell tells Popular Science. “From the field of agriculture, we learn a lot about animal physiology and how animals work, and can then design diets with the ingredients we have for specific purposes.”

In addition to bringing in knowledge from across different scientific disciplines, the team collaborates with other accredited zoos, aquariums, and universities to share research and data on animal nutrition. They’ve published studies on animals from bigger animals like zebras and rhinos, to smaller fish and amphibians, which is crucial to filling in nutritional gaps. If the team is not sure what a particular species needs to eat in order to thrive, they will turn to comparative nutrition for answers.

“We go with a close relative [and] take what we know about the animals we do know a lot about and apply that to some of our other species,” Bissell explains. “Then we learn from our own animals by assessing how they’re doing on the diets that we’re offering, so we can gauge their nutritional status and make adjustments as needed.”

Staying nimble and making these adjustments is also important. If a supply chain issue disrupts what the nutrition team can get, having a back-up plan that includes nutritious food is critical. If an animal is familiar and comfortable with at least a few types of food, they will generally fare better, whether there are shortages or not.

At the same time, the nutrition team works to ensure that the food and its presentation mimics life in the wild as much as possible.

“Animals in the wild are spending their days solving puzzles, trying to figure out how to eat, while staying away from predators or toxins,” Bissell says. “They’re making a lot of decisions all day, so if we just offered them food in a bowl that would not provide them with mental stimulation.”

One of the most common behaviors is foraging, or digging through obstacles like grass, mud, or leaves to find food. The dishes the team creates are often presented in a way that encourages foraging, so that the animals keep up those natural behaviors. Leaves will be hung up in a tree for the giraffes to eat as they would in the wild. Carnivores like lions will get whole prey and bones to eat, which also helps keep their own jaws and teeth healthy. The team also pays attention to seasonal shifts to keep animals in their natural rhythm.

“Probably the biggest group of animals that we do this with would be birds,” says Bissell. “If they’re laying eggs, they might need more calcium, so we might add sources of calcium into their diet.”

Surprisingly, feeding bigger animals like lions and elephants is not as challenging as making sure that the insectivores have enough to eat. True to their name, anteaters almost exclusively eat bugs, and can consume up to 3,000 insects per day. To keep up with all of those the bugs, Bissell and the team work side-by-side with manufacturers to ensure their insect pellets meet the physical and nutritional standards needed to align with insects the anteaters encounter in the wild. To supplement, the anteaters will also get a bit of produce with the insects, since they do also eat fruit.

“We do a lot with like ice cakes, where we can freeze food in blocks of ice and can color the water with like vegetable dyes, so it’s fun and engaging. And the ice, especially in Florida in the summer, is really nice for hydration,” Bissell explains. “We are often pulling from what’s already in the animal diet or similar things, because just like humans, it’s not a great idea to just add a bunch of stuff on top of your existing diet.”

They’ll also follow themes, from a little fall pies to a driver’s license out of fruit and leaves for a gorilla’s 16th birthday and a food sculpture shaped like a margarita for a 21st birthday. That devotion to keeping meals fresh and creative helps all animals, humans included.

“I like making animals’ lives better, and by extension people’s lives better, because we care about these animals so much,” says Bissell.

#4636. The 2027 BMW 740 xDrive Builds on Excellence

Revised design and an updated interior sharpen the case for BMW’s biggest executive sedan.

BMW’s 7-series has been in a race with the Mercedes-Benz S-class for nearly 50 years over the German executive sedan crown. But an avant-garde, new-generation reimagining in 2022 knocked the long-wheelbase sedan off its pedestal. Four years later, BMW has tweaked the 7-series’s front and rear design and upgraded the interior with better technology. Also, it’s lost the “i” from the end of its badge, as part of BMW’s new policy on model naming. Can a shorter name, a prettier face, and new screens push it back into contention?

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The 2027 BMW 740 xDrive’s most significant change is apparent at first glance. Horizontal grille slats inside the sizable kidney grille replace the previous vertical ones. Split headlights stick around, with a new vertical, indented integration below the daytime running lights. Extended LED taillights are also new for 2027. Inside, the BMW 740 receives much of the same treatment that’s been given to the Neue Klasse EV models, including a new four-spoke steering wheel, a snappier operating system, and a sleek panoramic display.

Engine: turbocharged and mild-hybridized 2998-cc inline-six

Transmission: 8-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

In the hills above Lake Elsinore, the 740 xDrive showed off just how magically BMW’s adaptive chassis control system is, especially in its more able Professional guise. This uses full air suspension and active roll stabilization through an electrical system that applies torque against the sway bars to counter lean under cornering loads. So equipped, the 7-series rewarded a spirited pace on California canyon roads, despite a 4800-pound curb weight sitting atop a 126.6-inch wheelbase.

Front-end turn-in was sharp, and the minuscule amount of body roll effectively hid the magnitude of weight swinging around. Like many recent BMWs, the steering was nicely weighted but largely mute, forcing dynamic awareness to come from the base of the seat instead of through my fingers. While plentiful electronically ordered handling adjustments were no doubt happening in real time, these intrusions felt imperceptible behind the wheel.

But the 740 isn’t a one-trick pony, either. Out on the highway, the 7-series serves a different customer. The same roll stabilization technology that keeps it planted in the canyons can decouple the roll bars for straight-line driving, reducing unwanted movements in the cabin and allowing the air suspension to soften even more. The result was a ride that felt effortlessly smooth over freeway joints but never turned wallowing. Luxury vehicles shouldn’t translate bumps and dips inside the cabin, and the 740 expertly balances stability at the wheel with a supple experience in the rear seat. Cruising at California highway speeds was where the 7-series felt truly at home.

Similarly, the turbocharged and electrified 3.0-liter inline-six engine is powerful and smooth, but certainly not shouty. With 394 hp, the 740 has the same power as a base-model X5, but it didn’t feel lacking at the helm. The 398-lb-ft torque peak comes in at 1850 rpm, which pushed the big sedan along gracefully without apparent effort. But winding the engine to the 5200 rpm at which peak power arrives elicited a pleasant, if speaker-amplified, song—although it felt largely unnecessary given the muscle of the torque curve.

Paired with the ever-amicable ZF eight-speed automatic transmission, the powertrain of the 740 felt like a means to an end rather than a especial highlight, but that’s how most buyers of large luxury sedans will expect it to be. Sure, you can paddle-shift through the gears and enjoy the gearbox’s satisfyingly snappy responses, but how many owners are likely to regularly do so?

BMW is proud of its hands-free Highway Assistant semiautonomous driving system, and so I put this to the test on I-5 South. The SAE Level 2 system can drive hands-free up to 85 mph as long as you keep a forward gaze, and it did so well. From slowing for construction zones to autonomous lane changes, the semiautonomous system handled busy California traffic smartly and smoothly.

My only real complaint with the updated 7-series was its soft brake pedal. Even with the sizable standard rotors, the soft pedal tuning made the heavy sedan feel underbraked, requiring more force than I was expecting to need to apply for a quick stop. Plus, like most of the R&T team who have encountered it, I don’t like the new four-spoke steering wheel with its strange disconnected spokes and awkward haptic touch controls.

With a mild facelift and the same powertrains as before, the 2027 7-series’s most noticeable upgrades are all inside. BMW uses many buzzwords and acronyms to describe the new interior experience, but the most important one is the Panoramic iDrive system. As in the X5, iX3, i3, and new 3-series, the Neue Klasse direction has removed the old physical iDrive controller and replaced it with a fully touchscreen system. The 7-series now has a 17.9-inch central screen, a recessed 14.6-inch passenger display, and the long panoramic gauge cluster that sits atop the dashboard.

In practice, the new user experience was a mixed bag. I’m quick to criticize any vehicle that lacks tactile controls, and the glamour of BMW’s new system doesn’t belie this fault. Save for a scrolling volume control near the nub shifter, everything from climate control to vehicle settings must be manipulated through the central touchscreen. The screen responds quickly and has a permanent menu with obvious icons for climate control, vehicle settings, navigation, and media inputs. However, tapping on any of these icons once is only the start of a multistep process, much of which will be done with eyes off the road.

To adjust the suspension or ride height on the 740, I had to click through four menus before the change was complete. Even the seat’s lumbar support has to be adjusted through the touchscreen. That’s a bridge too far in my book.

Despite these annoyances, BMW’s new system mostly excels at providing driving information with the projected gauge cluster. Illuminated on a span of masked glass across the dashboard, this instrument display was perfectly placed and kept my field of vision clear. BMW’s projection direction is smartly tuned, with speed placed directly in front of the driver and navigation to the right. Interesting but superfluous information like elevation is projected nearer to the passenger side. My only real complaint was a hard-to-decipher tachometer.

My Frozen Purple 740 xDrive was well appointed with white Merino leather seats that were heated, cooled, and massaging. The seating experience was unimpeachably comfortable except for the loud fan noise while using the ventilation function. Seating adjustment is now done through door-mounted buttons, allowing BMW to make the seats even wider. The equipped Dolby Atmos system was predictably excellent, and interior sound levels were nearly silent even without active tunes.

As brands like Audi and Lexus move away from the ultraluxury sedan market, BMW’s 7-series is left with a single natural competitor—the Mercedes-Benz S-class. But the fight isn’t exactly equal, either. The 740 starts at $101,350 in a rear-wheel-drive configuration, while the most affordable S-class starts at $114,100. Mercedes offers more horsepower and torque for the money, but the luxury-sedan buyer is unlikely to be motivated exclusively by performance.

Of course, if they are, then the 740 sits at the base of the range, with both the hybrid 750e and twin-turbo V-8 M760 positioned above it. Plus, of course, the continued novelty of the fully electric i7 EV, which shares the same bodywork.

Far be it from me to pretend reviewing a BMW 7-series is hard work, but the massaging seat feature certainly helped me calm down after hours of driving. BMW offers a variety of intensity settings and location-focused massages, meaning you can tailor the experience to where you need it most. It isn’t too hard or unnatural-feeling, and it still provides genuine relief.

#4635. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4634. Mercedes-Benz Asks: What If We Put Screens in a Car’s Windows, Too?

New window display technology could unlock the opportunity to include even more screens in Mercedes automobiles.

If there’s a space to insert a screen, the folks at Mercedes-Benz will find it. And turns out, the carmaker’s engineers have found what they consider the next frontier to be conquered: your car’s windows. On Tuesday, Mercedes released previews of two new types of window displays, one called Intelligent Display in Glass and the other named Holographic Display.

The “Intelligent Display in Glass” essentially puts LED display elements directly into the vehicle windows. Why? Mercedes says warning symbols or traffic-related information could be displayed on the rear window to warn those behind you. One might presume brake lights do the trick of letting folks know you’re slowing down, but the examples Mercedes shows are much more specific as to the reason you’re slowing down; the glass can project the symbol of a car accident, pedestrian crossing, or all sorts of other things.

Our favorite is the text that simply reads “KEEP DISTANCE.” Could that potentially just enrage a tailgater even more? Sure, but it’s also objectively funny to have your car tell people behind you to back off.

Mercedes says it’s investigating two different LED technologies for this application. Mini LEDs are best-suited to larger displays in the rear window; meanwhile, Micro LEDs could be used on smaller areas to show animations, thanks to their higher resolution capabilities.

Examples of Micro LEDs in action are shown in the side window screens, where the car can display messages to its driver like battery charge status or a simple “goodbye” as you walk away. In both cases, when no content is displayed, Mercedes says the display elements laminated into the glass composite “remain almost invisible.” The “almost” there gives us some pause, so we’ll have to see it in person in order to make a judgement.

The other tech Mercedes previewed is the Holographic Display, which looks a bit like a HUD on steroids. A projector in the instrument panel would project content onto a new windshield that uses a special transparent film laminated into the glass. Mercedes says the display will be viewable only at specific viewing angles—the driver wouldn’t be able to see what’s projected in front of the passenger, and vice versa. The carmaker says this means the passenger could be watching a film projected onto the windshield, while the driver is shown navigation information.

In pictures, at least it’s better than a HUD in that the display looks like a projection you might see in a home theater setup. You get full color and a sharp image, though the examples that the carmaker showcases aren’t exactly too enticing, being images of Mercedes vehicles and the weather.

Just like the other displays shown in this preview, Mercedes says all of these ideas simply demonstrate potential future approaches. None of them are likely to end up in a production car any time soon, as they’re all currently under development. That said, now would be the time to sound off and let Mercedes know if any of the above is something you’d want in a car one day ... or not.

#4633. NASA teases experimental X-70 ‘Fractal’ aircraft

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

NASA has unveiled its next experimental aircraft, dubbed the X-70 Fractal. Well, “unveiled” may be a bit of a stretch. During this week’s UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman announced plans for the “crewed, high-performance platform” designed to boost maneuverability, flight control, and “other cutting-edge technologies in real flight.”

Beyond that, you’re guess is probably about as good as anyone’s. Even X-70’s sole visual hint may mean nothing at all. The shadowy frame seen silhouetted by fog in NASA’s announcement is explicitly identified as AI “generated content.” This means even the rounded cockpit, splayed tail fins, and extended wings may ultimately not even show up in the final design.

Despite a lack of photographs, NASA did provide some more concrete details about the X-70. The aircraft will have a 10,000 pound takeoff weight and will cruise at Mach .75 (about 570 miles per hour) at a maximum altitude of 45,000 feet. Its operational range is also expected to exceed 1,500 nautical miles (1,726 miles).

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” NASA Research and Technology Mission Directorate director Laurie Grindle said in the agency’s announcement. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

NASA also emphasized the X-70’s modular construction, which will allow quick swaps of internal and external payloads. As The War Zone noted, these features are likely intended to facilitate tests of experimental autonomous deployments and drone technology. The X-70 may also feature “bleeding-edge” abilities like morphing wings and “air-burst” controls, which allow aircraft to precisely maneuver midflight solely through blasts of pressurized air.

Isaacman said he expects the X-70 to complete its first flight within the next two years, although it’s always useful to take experimental aircraft timelines with a grain of salt. When NASA awarded Lockheed Martin the contract to develop its X-59 aircraft in 2016, the aim was to have a vehicle ready for testing by 2020. The actual X-59’s maiden flight ultimately took place on October 28, 2025.

#4632. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Learn the basics to keeping your heart healthy

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

“Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”

#4631. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

While it picked up most of the dust and dirt on the floor mats, it left behind pet fur and debris. The vacuum includes three attachments that are helpful in harder-to-reach spots: The crevice tool worked well, but the brush tool didn’t do much for puppy fur. A flexible connection hose also acts as an extended hose, but it seemed to diminish the suction power when added. It’s not as powerful as the others we tested, which makes sense given its size.

I liked that an additional air filter was included. Depending on how often you use the vacuum, the filters can last up to six months without needing a change, but it’s nice that an extra one is provided.

Overall, the DetailVac is convenient and great for quick cleanups or accidents. I think it would be especially helpful if you have kids.

The Bissell Garage Pro Wall-Mounted Wet/Dry Vacuum is for anyone serious about keeping their car and garage clean. Mounted on your wall with a 32-foot hose, it delivers strong 12-amp suction to tackle dirt and wet spills. There’s a blower option, perfect for drying off a freshly washed Porsche, which I did with stellar results.

Even at its size, assembly was simple. Once it’s together, it performs at the level you’d expect from a professional detailing station. This is the best pick if you have the room and use a vacuum in your garage often. It’s a full-service garage vacuum built to take a beating and deliver strong suction for any surface of your vehicle.

What also sets it apart is its auto-tool kit, which includes attachments—crevice tools, upholstery brushes, and a wet nozzle for moisture cleanup—for every cleaning scenario.

Whether you’re an obsessive detailer or just want a cleaner ride, the Garage Pro delivers. It is powerful, versatile, and a worthwhile addition to any garage.

Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum packs a lot of power for a smaller unit. I quickly understood why most people use the wall-mount option; not only does it help keep the 30-foot hose out of the way, but it also helps keep your garage organized. If I had mounted this, the hose probably would’ve been less cumbersome to maneuver. Drilling holes in our space to mount several vacuums was not an option, but we did our best to re-create this real-world scenario. Assembly was a bit of a struggle—especially getting the central hose in—but I might not have used enough force initially. My advice would be to use all your strength; I promise you won’t break it.

The suction is decent, with 120 volts of power, but the attachments really help this vacuum shine: steel telescoping wand, bare-floor tool, snake wand, crevice tool, elongated dust brush, and upholstery tool. They make this vacuum even more versatile, allowing you to tackle everything from floor mats to delicate surfaces efficiently.

Using this vacuum was genuinely satisfying, like power-washing your interior with suction. Adam’s did indeed get the job done fast, and had it been wall-mounted, I think I would’ve seen its overall appeal, since using the hose would likely be more manageable. Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum is worth every penny for those who love organization.

The Shark StainForce isn’t your typical car vacuum, and that’s precisely why we wanted to include it. Rather than tackling loose dirt, this cordless spot cleaner focuses on stubborn oil stains, soda spills, and odors embedded in your car’s carpeting.

There’s a three-step cleaning process involved, but it’s well worth the extra work. Spray the affected area with Shark’s dual-activated cleaning solution, scrub with the included attachment, and use the vacuum’s suction to extract the mess. The dual-chamber formula mixes when sprayed, helping break down stains without requiring any measuring or extra preparation. Two attachments, including a crevice tool, make it easier to reach tight spaces around seats and other interior surfaces.

Weighing under three pounds, the StainForce is easy to maneuver, and its cordless design eliminates the hassle of finding an outlet. The included storage caddy keeps everything organized between cleanups.

There are a few limitations. Battery life topped out at approximately 20 minutes when we tested (so it still works fine for spot cleaning). Also, you’ll need to purchase Shark’s own cleaning solution when the included supply runs out.

For drivers regularly battling coffee spills, muddy footprints, or pet accidents, the StainForce offers a convenient, targeted cleaning solution.

A high-quality vacuum cleaner can make all the difference for keeping your car’s interior spotless. Unlike household vacuums, car-specific models are designed to tackle heavier debris in tight spaces. However, with so many options available, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. It’s important to consider key features that affect performance and convenience to make an informed decision.

Three of the most crucial factors to evaluate are suction power, which determines how effectively the vacuum picks up dirt; attachments and accessories, which help clean hard-to-reach areas; and the power source, which impacts portability and run time.

Understanding these features will help you find a vacuum that best suits your needs, whether you prioritize strong suction for deep cleaning, versatile tools for detail work, or the malleability of a hose. Let’s dive into these essential features to ensure you choose the right car vacuum cleaner for the job.

Suction power is the most critical factor in a car vacuum because vehicle interiors can become a nightmare with everything we drag in and out of them. Unlike home carpets, car surfaces are filled with a million little spaces, textured upholstery, and stubborn floor mats that anything you can think of clings to. A vacuum with weak suction won’t be able to extract dirt that’s ground into these surfaces, leaving your car looking only half clean. Not ideal.

Additionally, higher suction power means faster, more efficient cleaning. Instead of repeatedly going over the same spot, a strong vacuum gets the job done in fewer passes, saving you time and effort. It also helps tackle heavier things such as leaves, sand, or pebbles. If you take your car’s cleanliness seriously (or don’t want to spend forever vacuuming), a high-powered vacuum is the way to go.

Attachments and accessories are essential in a car vacuum because car interiors are full of tight spaces and tricky surfaces that a standard nozzle can’t handle. Unlike home vacuums, which deal with flat carpets and open areas, a car vacuum must navigate between seats, air vents, and cup holders, all of which require specialized tools.

For example, a crevice tool helps reach between and along door panels, while a brush attachment is perfect for loosening dust from dashboards. Wide nozzles quickly work on large areas like a trunk, and wet/dry tools handle accidents before they become permanent stains. The right attachments don’t just make cleaning easier; they ensure you’re getting every last crumb out of your ride, leaving it truly spotless.

The power source of a car vacuum determines its suction strength, mobility, and convenience. Corded (AC-powered) vacuums offer the strongest suction but require an outlet and may limit movement. Cordless (battery-powered) models provide maximum portability for quick cleanups but often have weaker suction and limited run time.

Vacuums that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet are great for on-the-go use but generally lack the power of AC models. Choosing the right type depends on your needs, such as going corded for power, cordless for convenience, or 12-volt for in-car accessibility.

The ThisWorx portable car vacuum routinely came up as the one to avoid. Its low suction didn’t do much, leaving most of the dirt and dust behind. While it is inexpensive, you do indeed get what you pay for.

The same goes for generic no-name vacuums on Amazon. While they are more affordable, they are also unreliable and often break within months of purchase.

We focused on suction power, attachments, and ease of use for this test. Using substantially dirty floor mats as our starting point, we taped them off to determine which vacuum was the most powerful. These mats were full of dirt, dust, pebbles, and dog fur; they were pretty much littered with what you might encounter in your vehicle. This strategy helped us quickly determine which vacuums were up to the task.

Our garage in New Brunswick, New Jersey, was the ideal backdrop for this test. Not only was it still dirty from summer trips, it also allowed me to spread out the old and very used floor mats I’d be using. While this test focused on how effectively the vacuums would clean up cars, a happy surprise was that they also cleaned the garage.

For this test, we reached out to pros to see what products they prefer. After determining fan favorites, digging around forums, and connecting with detailers we’ve worked with in the past, we devised a list of items to review. (You know you’re headed in the right direction when you hear the same brand or product come up multiple times.) This is how we arrived at Chemical Guys, Adam’s, Bissell, and Shark—solid and reliable brands. Metrovac popped up in my digging as a reliable shop vac in a popular Reddit group (r/AutoDetailing). They weren’t wrong.

We didn’t look at handheld car vacuums in this test. While they’re tops for convenience, they would be a separate category to investigate, given their variety. We did keep convenience in mind when picking the units we wanted to focus on, but this test was done with serious garage owners and car enthusiasts in mind.

When we reviewed the Car+Boat from Dyson, we were immensely impressed at how well the mini-vac lived up to its brand’s legacy. With legendary suction power, the Dyson was as much a revelation for car lovers as the company’s larger vacuums were for homeowners all those years ago.

Portable, lightweight, and affordable. What more could you want in a car vac? With a 20-volt MAX Li-ion battery and extra-long crevice tool, it’s as great for the car as it is around the house.

Looking for a little more power than a portable cordless vacuum can provide? Pick up this mini-utility shop vac from Armor All. It’s far more convenient than lugging around a larger shop vac, has a washable filter, and doubles as a blower.

When choosing a car or garage vacuum, size and capacity are crucial factors that impact performance and convenience. A vacuum with anywhere from two to six gallons of capacity is usually sufficient for car detailing, providing enough volume for typical debris while remaining lightweight and portable. Smaller vacuums are easier to maneuver inside a car and can be stored conveniently in a garage or trunk.

A 10-plus-gallon shop vacuum is better for garage use or frequent heavy-duty cleaning. These larger models can handle bigger messes, including sawdust, metal shavings, and wet spots, without requiring frequent emptying. They also typically feature more powerful motors for increased suction. However, they take up more storage space and may be less portable. If you need a balance between power and maneuverability, a mid-size vacuum can provide strong suction without being too bulky.

While a regular household vacuum might seem convenient for cleaning your car or garage, it often lacks the necessary power, durability, and specialized attachments for effective cleaning in these environments. Household vacuums are designed primarily for indoor surfaces such as carpets and hardwood floors, meaning they may struggle to pick up messes commonly found in cars and garages. Their shorter hoses and bulkier designs can make it challenging to reach tight spaces.

Dedicated car vacuums and shop vacuums are better suited for these tasks, offering more powerful suction, longer hoses, and attachments specifically designed for automotive cleaning. These vacuums are built with durability, often featuring rugged designs that can withstand dust, moisture, and rough handling in a garage setting. While household vacuums may work in a pinch for light cleaning, investing in a purpose-built car or garage vacuum ensures more efficient cleaning and a longer-lasting machine.

HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters are essential when purchasing a car or garage vacuum, especially if you are concerned about air quality. Standard vacuum filters may struggle to trap fine particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander, and mold spores, which can get released back into the air during cleaning.

HEPA filters, however, are designed to capture at least 99.97 percent of particles, making them highly effective at reducing allergens and airborne contaminants. This is particularly beneficial if you suffer from allergies.

For car and garage cleaning, a HEPA or high-efficiency filtration system can also help keep your vehicle’s interior and your garage workspace cleaner by preventing fine dust from resettling. While HEPA-filtered vacuums may be slightly more expensive, they offer significant benefits for maintaining a healthier environment.

#4629. Baby whale surprises scientists

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:33 AM EST

The 2027 North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) baby season has officially begun. The calving season lasts from November through April, and is a particularly important stretch of time given that the species is classified as critically endangered by the IUCN Red List.

Due to their low numbers, scientists are closely monitoring these baleen whales. Yet even with all of that surveillance, one whale managed to keep a secret up until September.Experts spotted a known female and her previously unidentified calf from last calving season near Anticosti Island, Quebec, Canada, according to the New England Aquarium.

The 38-year-old female right whale is called Silt. In addition to being a mother, Silt is  also a grandmother and great-grandmother. The new calf is her sixth baby known to scientists.

“Silt managed to fly under the radar of survey teams throughout the spring and summer,” according to the aquarium “Although we don’t know exactly when or where her calf was born, she was briefly seen in the southeastern United States calving grounds in February, so it’s possible the calf was born there.”

More North Atlantic right whales are always good news. They are one of the most endangered large whales, and are vulnerable to ship collisions and fishing gear entanglement. Almost exactly a year ago, we were happy to report that the species is showing signs of slowly rebounding. 2024’s estimate of around 384 North Atlantic right whales represents a 2.1 percent increase from 2023’s estimate.

“The population increase is really good news, and so far, what we’ve seen in 2025 is also good news,” New England Aquarium senior scientist Heather Pettis told Popular Science in October 2025 . But “we’re talking about a population of 384 individual whales—that’s still incredibly low,” she added. “Yes, we’re seeing increases. They’re small, and we still are seeing injuries to animals from human activities. And so, you know, I say that we’re cautiously optimistic.”

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

#4627. New Food Pyramid Puts Healthy Carbs and Plant-Based Foods First

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This new food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

The new pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

The new pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The new pyramid highlights three guidelines:

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the new international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The new international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

While the new pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

The differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the new pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

While both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the new pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

Routhenstein noted that an important distinction is that this new pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein said.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the new pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:

The pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is important to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein said.

#4625. Scientists detect ‘pregnant’ coral using ultrasound device

Published Nov 6, 2026 12:47 PM EST

Scientists have a new tool in the fight to save Earth’s endangered coral reefs and it’s something many moms-to-be know all too well: the ultrasound.

This week, veteran camera-maker Canon announced its high-tech ultrasound platform can scan living coral submerged underwater and detect eggs developing inside them. Until now, checking whether coral was carrying eggs typically required cutting it open. This ultrasound development means researchers can assess coral reproduction non-invasively for the first time. By using ultrasound, scientists can gather crucial information about a coral’s reproductive health and try to predict when it will release its eggs. That insight can help conservationists time and target their restoration efforts without damaging or sacrificing the species in the process.

Canon conducted the experiment in collaboration with United Kingdom-based conservation organization Coral Spawning International (CSI). The team used Canon’s Aplio i700, an advanced medical ultrasound system normally used on humans in hospital settings. In this case though, it scanned six species of large polyp stony coral with varying skeletal structures. The device’s powerful mixture of high and ultra high frequency probes let researchers see through the coal’s skeletons and view their internal structures. The team verified their results by cutting open one coral species, Trachyphyllia geoffroyi, and taking high powered images of its interior. Those images were then cross referenced with the results from the ultrasound, confirming that the structure identified in the scan were indeed eggs.

“This experiment demonstrates that imaging innovation has the power to show us what was previously unseen, creating a deeper understanding of the world around us,” Canon EMEA Sustainability and Government Affairs Director Peter Bragg said in a statement. “By unlocking this knowledge, we hold a fundamental belief that imaging has the power to transform the world.”

Coal can use all the help it can get. Late last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) released a sobering assessment warning that nearly all (96 percent) of the Earth’s coral reef ecosystem face an extremely high risk of collapse within the next 50 years. The main culprit? Warming oceans and heat waves brought on by climate change.

That dire threat isn’t just a problem for coral, either. Coral reefs, sometimes referred to as the “rainforests of the sea” are the among the most biodiverse eco systems on the planet and support an estimated quarter of all marine species. When reefs collapse, the coral dies and is replaced by algae and sponges which are not able to support as diverse a range of marine life. As a result, the ocean’s overall biological health ebbs and flows alongside coral.

Understanding when corals will spawn can give scientists critical data for breeding and a leg up on restoration efforts, which can help them try and tip the odds in  coral’s favor. Ultrasound scans could make that work more precise while sparing the coral from an untimely dissection.

#4624. Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

“[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, said Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

“[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

“It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” said Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”

Bitner said women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she said. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”

In fact, Bitner said providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart plans to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she said.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

“My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she said. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical company Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

“It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart said.

In everyday life, Bitner said that while some patients avoid talking about midlife issues like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

As more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” said Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her issue because we know it’s not.”

#4623. Mercedes CTO: Level 3 Autonomy Ambitions Were ‘Early,’ Focus Turns to Level 2++

The new S-Class sets back the self-driving clock a little, but that might not be such a bad thing.

Mercedes-Benz’s autonomy roadmap has been a bit jumbled as of late. It was well over three years ago that the company’s Level 3 Drive Pilot automated driving system was approved to operate in Nevada, making it the first Level 3 system available in the U.S.

Those were exciting times on the surface, but with a hard speed limit of about 40 mph, the actual use case of the system wasn’t so great for American roads. A couple of years have since gone by from when Drive Pilot launched on the EQS and S-Class, so one might expect that Mercedes has taken those years to expand the system’s capability to higher speeds. That’s not exactly what’s been happening, though. Instead, the refreshed S-Class launched this year without Level 3 Drive Pilot capability at all. So, what gives?

In a recent media roundtable, Mercedes-Benz CTO Jörg Burzer explained how Mercedes’s thinking has evolved. “Level 3 ... so, what we did is, we were the first ones bringing Level 3 on the street in the U.S. and in Germany,” Burzer started. “And sometimes if you are too early, then you see that you have to work on what the customer really wants. And the challenge we had is facing the usability of the system.”

Rolling out a Level 3 highway system that was only capable of working at speeds typically reserved for urban streets, well, it sort of defeats the purpose. Yes, it was great for traffic jams, but Mercedes itself admits this Level 3 system was just too early.

“And then obviously we realized that we have to expand the ODD [Operation Design Domain]. We have to make it faster and from the speed level, but also we worked on the sensor set, and we learned a lot,” Burzer said. “And this was then fitting into everything we do, our normal hands-free, with Level 2++ [autonomy].

What’s up with the “Level 2++” talk? It’s the small step back Mercedes is taking from Level 3. Arguably, the Level 2++ system shipping on the S-Class and more new Mercedes models will be more helpful than the Level 3 it offered previously. However, being Level 2, it puts the onus and responsibility of the car back on the driver behind the wheel. With the Drive Pilot’s Level 3 operation, you could legally text or otherwise be completely disengaged from the driving experience with it activated.

Being able to go hands-free on the highway at high speeds is a driver assistance feature offered by all sorts of automakers today. Burzer recognizes how important it is for Mercedes to be competitive in this market, hence the switch to an extremely capable Level 2 system. The real trick will be rolling out in the months ahead, as the “++” part of the system allows for true point-to-point autonomous navigation on city streets. You’ll still need to pay attention, but the car should be able to do most of the work for you.

That’s the level Mercedes intends to stay at until it cracks Level 4, too. Instead of ramping back up to Level 3, Burzer believes it’s best to skip all the way toward Level 4, where you’d be able to do anything in the driver’s seat. “So we have, in the S-Class, up to 27 sensors for Level 2++,” Burzer said. “With this experience, we basically also decided, let's go for Level 4.”

But it’ll be a long time before Level 4 autonomous driving is available on a Mercedes-Benz vehicle, Burzer says he believes. Sometime after 2030 is his current best prediction. And when it does arrive, expect the features to roll out slowly, with urban driving being the last to fully come online.

#4622. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

Excellent. There are so many warehouses around here, it always baffled me that they weren't all covered with solar panels. Next we gotta get to work on all the parking lots.

Faropoint and SolarKal have not yet announced completion dates, subscription prices, or enrollment details for their New Jersey warehouse roof community solar portfolio.
